\subsubsection{Rules for a Record}\label{sss:eis-rules}

A calibration impedance is required, for the four independent reasons above, and
it must be switchable across decades. These seven rules are what a record needs
beyond it, and each carries the measured cost of ignoring it.

\begin{enumerate}[nosep]
  \item \textbf{Choose an excitation code pair that does not cross a major
    carry.} Both codes inside one octave delivers the commanded amplitude to
    \SI{0.06}{\percent}; a pair spanning eight bits is out by
    \SI{1.5}{\percent}, and at the \SI{4}{\milli\volt} excitation a carry at the
    most significant bit costs \SI{3.5}{\percent}
    (Table~\ref{tab:eis-excitation}).
  \item \textbf{Use the two-level excitation where the record is dense.} Sampled
    densely the measured impedance is the same as a synthesised sine's to five
    significant figures, and the square delivers \(1.28\times\) the fundamental
    for the same interface excursion. Sampled at the \num{32} conversions per
    channel per period a converter reading two channels can deliver, it costs
    \SI{2.99}{\degree} of phase and the sine costs nothing
    (Section~\ref{sss:eis-excitation}).
  \item \textbf{Start the record only after the electrode's own dc transient has
    decayed.} An eight-cycle record taken at the excitation onset reads
    \(-\SI{2.0}{\percent}\) at \SI{1}{\kilo\hertz} and
    \(-\SI{1.3}{\percent}\) at \SI{10}{\kilo\hertz} on a load whose step time
    constant \(\tau = C_{\mathrm{dl}}(R_u \parallel R_{\mathrm{ct}})\) is
    \SI{0.99}{\milli\second} (Figure~\ref{fig:eis-settling}). The excess decays
    as \(\exp(-t/\tau)\) and is a
    function of \(t/\tau\) alone to better than \SI{1}{\percent} across a decade
    of \(\tau\) and a decade of frequency, so \textbf{wait \(5\tau\) for
    \SI{0.1}{\percent} and \(7\tau\) for \SI{0.01}{\percent}} ---
    \SI{99}{\micro\second}, \SI{0.99}{\milli\second} and \SI{9.9}{\milli\second}
    for the three electrodes. Averaging is not a substitute: sixteen cycles
    still leave \SI{1.2}{\percent}. Range the code before timing the record ---
    repeated on a code whose minimum measurable impedance is \(1.67\times\) the
    load, the same experiment reads \(+\SI{16}{\percent}\) and
    \(+\SI{74}{\percent}\), which is the output sitting on its rail and not
    settling at all.
  \item \textbf{Sample on a grid commensurate with the excitation}, by deriving
    the converter strobe and the excitation from the same divider. A grid
    \num{0.35} samples per period out of step costs \SI{0.6}{\percent} on a
    reactive load --- and reads correctly on a resistor, so a resistive
    self-check does not catch it.
  \item \textbf{Average with a boxcar rather than by discarding samples.} On a
    reactive load the \(n\)-th current harmonic is
    \(Z(f)/(n\,Z(nf))\) of the fundamental rather than \(1/n\), so the high
    orders fold into the fundamental bin: plain decimation to \num{135} samples
    per period is \(1.3\times\) worse than a boxcar and not monotonic in rate,
    and a record kept at \num{256} samples per period reads \SI{5}{\percent}
    high where the small-signal analysis says \SI{0.03}{\percent}.
  \item \textbf{Measure the feedback resistance on every chip; never compute it.}
    The law \(\SI{18}{\kilo\ohm} + \SI{6}{\kilo\ohm}\,N\) is already
    \SI{9.1}{\percent} low at \(N = 0\) at the nominal point --- the
    closed-switch stack of Section~\ref{ss:tiarprog}, and within
    \SI{0.5}{\percent} at every code above \(N = 20\)
    (Table~\ref{tab:eis-coverage}) --- and it carries \(\sigma =
    \SI{11}{\percent}\) of process spread on top of that, so storing it costs
    \(\sigma = \SI{10.2}{\percent}\) of measured magnitude. One dc measurement
    per chip takes that to \SI{0.0006}{\percent}
    (Section~\ref{sss:eis-accuracy}). Gain constants are per die, not per design.
  \item \textbf{Rotate the phase by \(180\,f/f_s\) when one converter reads both
    channels.} Interleaving them samples the two half a conversion apart, which
    costs that angle on a two-level excitation --- \SI{2.81}{\degree} at
    \SI{13.6}{\kilo\hertz} and \num{64} conversions per period. The rotation is
    exact and needs no calibration; without it the \(\pm\SI{0.573}{\degree}\)
    gate caps the excitation at \SI{2.77}{\kilo\hertz}, half the band the
    amplifiers support.
\end{enumerate}
